title: Severe Hypothyroidism Presenting as Rhabdomyolysis and Acute Kidney Injury: A Rare Case Report with Detailed Molecular Insights
content: Background: Hypothyroidism, affecting 4–5% of adults globally, rarely progresses to rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury (AKI), with an incidence <1%. This case highlights an idiopathic presentation in a young male, elucidating molecular mechanisms driving this rare cascade. Case Presentation: A 28-year-old male presented with progressive muscle weakness, diffuse myalgia, fatigue, and marked cold intolerance, reporting doubled pain in colder environments. Examination showed 3/5 muscle weakness (Medical Research Council scale) without myxedema or goiter. Laboratory findings confirmed rhabdomyolysis (creatine phosphokinase: 4323 U/L, reference: 24–195 U/L), AKI (creatinine: 1.6 mg/dL, peaking at 1.9 mg/dL, reference: 0.7–1.3 mg/dL), mild hyperkalemia (K+ 5.6 mmol/L), hypocalcemia (Ca2+ 7.8 mg/dL), and myoglobinuria (dark urine, positive blood dipstick, no red blood cells). Severe hypothyroidism was identified (free T3: 0.26 pg/mL, reference: 2.3–4.2 pg/mL; free T4: 0.23 ng/dL, reference: 0.8–1.8 ng/dL; TSH: >150 µIU/mL, reference: 0.4–4.0 µIU/mL) without trauma, exercise, or statin triggers. Management and Outcome: Levothyroxine (50 µg daily, titrated) and aggressive intravenous saline (200–250 mL/hour) achieved full recovery within two weeks (creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL; CPK: 150 U/L; TSH: 5.2 µIU/mL), with resolution of muscle pain and fatigue. Conclusion: Severe hypothyroidism can disrupt mitochondrial ATP production, glycogen, and lipid metabolism, triggering rhabdomyolysis and AKI. Cold intolerance is a critical diagnostic clue. Routine thyroid function testing is essential in unexplained rhabdomyolysis or AKI, as timely intervention ensures complete recovery. Limitations include unavailable myoglobin and anti-TPO antibody testing.
